report.headline: Dead patent with a future (78/100, high confidence): a sodium-ion battery patent in a field that is still active, though crowded with later filings worth checking first.
report.what_it_is: This patent describes a rechargeable battery that moves sodium ions instead of lithium ions, using a phosphate-type cathode material and a carbon anode. Sodium is cheaper and more plentiful than lithium, which is why this chemistry draws interest for large stationary storage.

why_it_died.text: The owner, Valence Technology, paid the first two maintenance fees but skipped the third one, due at 11.5 years. The patent lapsed on 2017-03-29, about 5 years before its full term would have ended. The record shows no reinstatement. It appears to have lapsed through non-payment, not because a court or patent office ruled against it. The record does not say why the fee went unpaid. The 'died for money, not merit' signal scored only 5.2/15, so treat the reason as unclear.

case_for.point: The field still looks very alive. 214 later patents and applications cite this one, and examiners cited it against 127 later applications. That is why it scored a full 30/30 on 'field still alive'.

Interest kept going after the lapse. 33 filings by unrelated owners cite it with priority dates after 2017, and 6 date from 2019 or later. That includes Faradion, a sodium-ion company, alongside several universities.
Outside signals point to commercial interest in sodium-ion for cheap large-scale storage. A national lab is licensing hard-carbon anode tech, and recent research reports higher-voltage cathodes.
The patent was filed in 7 jurisdictions. That suggests the original owner saw real value in it at the time.

case_against.point: Most recent filers building on it are universities and research institutes, not companies. The market may still be maturing, not buying.
Citation counts measure technical interest, not sales. Heavy citation does not show that customers will pay for products based on this chemistry.
The shortest main claim is 194 words long, across 49 claims. This patent may work better as background reading than as a single clear product recipe.
The patent shares the idea, not the factory know-how. Expect to rebuild materials processing and cell-making details yourself.

blockers.point: Later patents by other owners may still be in force. Examiners cited 89 of them against this one, and they may cover improvements you would need. Worth checking with an attorney before building.
The original owner filed 2 later patents citing this one that may still be in force, such as US9269955B2 on manganese phosphate electrode materials.
Shipping and selling battery cells usually means UN 38.3 transport testing plus UL or IEC safety certification. That adds cost and time.
If your cathode material counts as a new chemical substance, US law may require an EPA premanufacture notice under TSCA before commercial manufacture.
Manufacturing know-how is not in the patent. Process development could be slow and costly.

assumption_to_test.assumption: Buyers of stationary storage, such as integrators or commercial and industrial site owners, will choose a sodium-ion phosphate-cathode product from a new startup for its lower cost and safety, despite lower energy density.
assumption_to_test.why_riskiest: The evidence shows strong technical and academic interest. It does not show paying demand, and recent filers are mostly universities. If buyers will not switch from lithium iron phosphate, there is no business, however open the chemistry appears to be.
assumption_to_test.how_to_test: In two weeks, interview 10-15 stationary-storage buyers or integrators about what price per kWh and what cycle life would make them trial sodium-ion. Ask what certifications they require. Also request one or two quotes from sodium-ion cell suppliers or contract manufacturers to compare costs. Budget: under $500 for outreach tools and a simple landing page.

attorney_questions: Of the 89 later patents by other owners cited against US6872492B2, and the 2 later Valence patents such as US9269955B2, which may still be in force and could cover the cathode or anode materials we plan to use?

Given that US6872492B2 lapsed for non-payment in 2017 with no reinstatement on record, is there any remaining risk it could be revived? Do any foreign family members in the 7 jurisdictions remain active in our target markets?
Would our planned sodium phosphate cathode material likely need a TSCA premanufacture notice, and how should we plan for that?
report.disclaimer: Research and triage only, not legal advice. This report is not a patentability, validity or freedom-to-operate opinion. Patent status shown here comes from public records that can lag or be wrong. An expired patent is not the same as free to use: follow-on patents, regulatory exclusivity, trade secrets and standards can still block a product. Confirm with a registered patent attorney before acting.

signals.signal: Sustained, broad technical interest: the patent is heavily cited, including by examiners, suggesting it sits near the foundation of sodium-ion phosphate cathode / carbon anode work.
Activity continued after the lapse, with dozens of unrelated filers building on it, though post-2019 citing activity is modest in absolute numbers.
Recent citing filers are mostly academic and research institutions, with one commercial sodium-ion developer (Faradion Ltd), pointing to a field still largely in R&D and early commercialization.

External market commentary describes sodium-ion as edging toward commercialization and as a cost-effective option for grid storage, and a national lab is actively licensing hard-carbon anode technology. This is a sign of an active ecosystem, not proof of revenue.

read.who_is_active: Since 2019, the filers citing this patent are Faradion Ltd and research institutions in China (Soochow University, Tongji University, Changchun Institute of Applied Chemistry), Korea (KAIST) and Russia (the Siberian solid-state chemistry institute), while Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Skoltech and Moscow State University appear in the market evidence.
read.market_read: Sodium-ion chemistry with polyanion cathodes and carbon anodes remains a live and growing area, judging by heavy cumulative citations, ongoing post-lapse filings and commentary about stationary-storage uses. Citation counts reflect technical interest rather than sales, and the long 194-word minimum independent claim and the mostly academic recent filers suggest this patent is best treated as background reference in a still-maturing market.

web.finding: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory is offering for licensing a technology for making high-capacity hard carbon for Na-ion batteries, published Nov 4, 2025, and describes sodium-ion batteries as a cost-effective option for large-scale storage.

pv magazine reported in 2022 that Skoltech and Moscow State University researchers developed high-voltage sodium-ion cathodes giving up to 15% higher energy density, and said sodium-ion batteries continue to edge toward commercialization.
